paras: The June 1919 Prairie Avenue bombings were dynamite explosions at buildings occupied by Black tenants on Prairie Avenue and nearby streets on the South Side of Chicago, followed by the arrest of a man found with a bomb. No one was reported hurt, and the damage fell on building entrances. Chicago's Black weeklies treated the arrest as a rare break in a run of bombings of Black homes, and the Chicago Whip used it to accuse a white property owners' association of directing the attacks.

According to the Whip, a property owners' association in the Kenwood and Hyde Park districts, built around twenty real estate dealers, aimed to keep Black residents out of the area "under the guise of keeping out undesirables." The paper alleged that the group planned to list property bought by Black buyers between Thirty-ninth and Fifty-first streets, press mortgage holders to "squeeze the Negroes out," and raise $96,000 a year from eight thousand white members.

The Chicago Broad-Ax reported that on a Wednesday night before 14 June, police answering a call about one explosion learned that a second bomb had been thrown nearby. The first wrecked the entrance of a two-story building at 5006-08 Calumet Avenue occupied by "colored tenants," and the second struck 5143-45 Prairie Avenue, "also occupied by colored people." The Chicago Defender of 21 June then reported "two more" explosions close together, at [5]145 Prairie Avenue and 19 East 47th Street with no one injured.

According to the Whip, on a Friday in June two officers from the fourth precinct station arrested a man about two blocks from explosions at 5143-45 Prairie Avenue and 5008 Calumet Avenue, moments after he was seen throwing away a package. The package, the Whip said, held a bomb of two sticks of dynamite with caps and fuses. The Defender named the arrested man as James Muchriel, an "Italian" whose right name was said to be Terranova, and said he had been employed by James Turris, a plumber on East 51st Street. The Whip did not name him but said he ran a plumbing shop in the real estate office of Dean & Meagher at 320 East 51st Street, whose partners it described as members of the Kenwood and Hyde Park property owners' association.

The Whip reported that Dean gave bond for the arrested man. No report of a hearing, indictment or trial appears in the coverage through mid-July. The Defender charged that police had been "so deliberate and brazenly neglectful" that they seemed to be "working in harmony with the bomb throwers."

Only Chicago's Black weeklies covered the case in the papers examined, and each gave it a different weight. The Broad-Ax ran the Calumet and Prairie bombings as a brief item, "Two Bombs Wake Up South Side; No One Hurt." The Defender's "Caught With Dynamite" presented the arrest as the first apparent break in the bombings and turned it into an attack on police laxity.

The Whip gave the case its front page under "Man Caught With Bomb in Hand Few Seconds After Explosion" and "Ninety Six Thousand Dollars to Fight Negroes." Claiming it had "finally succeeded in ascertaining who is directly responsible," the paper pointed to an organization headed by L. M. Smith, a real estate broker. Its editorial "Bombing the Bombers," citing "a very reliable source," held the Kenwood and Hyde Park Improvement Association largely responsible for the "bomb-war" on Black residents and warned that "THE BOMBERS WILL BE BOMBED." The same editorial listed kinds of Black people, among them politicians who preached submissiveness, whom it said deserved attack more than "the innocent, hardworking, home-buying, honest Negro," and told Smith that the "young, educated, progressive Negro" would deal with them.

The Broad-Ax placed the Calumet and Prairie bombings on a Wednesday night before 14 June, while the Whip put explosions at nearly the same addresses on a Friday whose date is missing from the printed text. The Defender paired the Prairie Avenue bombing with one at 19 East 47th Street rather than Calumet Avenue, leaving open whether the Whip joined an earlier bombing to the later arrest or whether the Prairie Avenue building was bombed twice.

reader.title: June 1919 Prairie Avenue bombings
bases: Bombs exploded at buildings occupied by Black tenants, damaging entrances and vestibules, with no one hurt (A2, A3, A6).

The Defender and the Whip independently report a Prairie Avenue bombing near 5145 and the arrest of a man with dynamite tied to a plumbing business on East 51st Street (A3, A6), and the Broad-Ax reports bombs at the same Prairie and Calumet addresses the Whip names (A2), though date and second address differ.

conflicts.note: The Whip's addresses match the Broad-Ax's Wednesday bombings, while its arrest matches the Defender's; the Whip may combine two nights, or the Prairie Avenue building may have been bombed twice. The record's 20 June is an inference from 'Friday', not a printed date.
All agree on Prairie Avenue near 5145; the second site differs.

record_check.dossier: Not printed: the Whip gives 'Friday, June —'; the Broad-Ax puts bombs at the same two addresses on a Wednesday night before 14 June; the Defender of 21 June reports the arrest. 20 June is plausible for the arrest night but unconfirmed, and the Calumet bombing may belong to the earlier night.

record_check.record: Bombs explode at 5143-45 Prairie Avenue and 5008 Calumet Avenue ...; police arrest a man carrying a dynamite bomb whom the Chicago Whip ties to a property owners' association
record_check.dossier: Supported by the Whip; the Defender names a different second site (19 East 47th St) and names the arrested man (James Muchriel, alias Terranova); the Broad-Ax dates the Calumet-Prairie bombings to a Wednesday before 14 June.
corroborated: the Defender and Broad-Ax also report the bombings, and the Defender the arrest.
One man arrested and accused (James Muchriel/Terranova per the Defender); the Whip alleges the Kenwood and Hyde Park property owners' association was behind the bombings.
